newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's PM raises stakes in general elections.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's PM raises stakes in general elections.

text.p: Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong raised the stakes on Wednesday in Singapore's general election, making clear his personal prestige and his party's authority rested on a strong showing in seats that are being contested.
The ruling People's Action Party (PAP) is already guaranteed a majority after the January 2 poll as 47 of parliament's 83 seats are not being contested by the opposition.
But on the hustings for the remaining 36 seats, Goh made it clear strong support in the contested areas is crucial to his government's credibility.

In a key constituency in the island's north, Cheng San, where the PAP faces a determined push by its old adversary the Worker's Party, Goh said the stakes in Thursday's polls were now "very, very high."

In comments reported in The Straits Times newspaper he told voters at a rally late on Tuesday to think carefully before the vote. "You are now deciding the future not just of Cheng San but also the future of Singapore, which way Singapore goes."
The PAP has dominated the government since independence in 1965 and faced no opposition members in parliament until 1981. In the outgoing parliament opposition parties hold four seats.
But this election has seen the introduction of some winner-take-all multi-member constituencies in which the victorious party could see up to six candidates elected.
A win in a multi-member constituency could sharply increase opposition representation in parliament and that could jeopardise Goh's premiership, according to some analysts.
This prospect is largely behind the battle for Cheng San, which has five seats at stake.
The PAP has launched an all-out assault on one Workers' Party (WP) candidate in the constituency, Tang Liang Hong. To vote against him means voting against the whole WP slate there.

PAP leaders have accused Tang of harbouring anti-Christian and communal Chinese views in a society that witnessed racial riots in the 1960s, and have threatened legal action against him for slander and libel after remarks made in a newspaper interview.
Tang was advised in letters from PAP lawyers that if he did not withdraw his remarks and apologise for them by 9 p.m. (1300 GMT) on Wednesday, legal action against him would proceed.
PAP leaders have not hesitated to take legal action against opposition figures in the past when they feel it is justified.

While campaigning on Wednesday, Low Thia Khiang, a Worker's Party leader, said the legal threat against Tang showed opposition parties and candidates face a great risk and pay a high price when they seek election, state television reported.

In a speech to another constituency, Goh made it clear that supporting the opposition could hit them where they live. He said the PAP would be monitoring results from every voting ward, which contain about 5,000 voters each, to pinpoint the precincts that supported them.
Using this information Goh said the government will determine which areas, even within individual constituencies, get priority for much sought after upgrading of their housing.

More than 80 percent of the population live in state-subsidised flats and government ministers have made it clear during the election campaign that voters would be far back in line for lavish renovation and development projects if they send an opposition politician to parliament.
The PAP tactics drew a comment from the United States.
"We believe that voters everywhere should be able to vote without fear of repercussions from governments as a result of their responsibilities as citizens," the State Department said.
